html:
An art movement in which Mexican painters covered the walls of public buildings with huge murals of their country's history and people, from the 1920s to the 1970s.

After the Mexican Revolution, the education minister José Vasconcelos began, from 1921, to hire artists to paint schools, ministries and other public buildings. Most Mexicans could not read, and the murals were meant to teach them a shared national story: the Indigenous past, the Spanish conquest, the struggles of workers and peasants.

Its three great names:

  • Diego Rivera, whose murals at the National Palace tell Mexico's history from the Aztecs onward.
  • José Clemente Orozco, darker and more tragic in tone.
  • David Alfaro Siqueiros, the most politically radical, who experimented with new paints and tools.

The movement also reached the United States. Rivera painted Detroit's car factories, and his mural at New York's Rockefeller Center was destroyed in 1934 because it showed Lenin. The New Deal paid for murals across America in a similar spirit. Frida Kahlo, Rivera's wife, followed her own path.
sum: An art movement in which Mexican painters covered the walls of public buildings with huge murals of their country's history and people, from the 1920s to the 1970s.
